newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh's industrial growth faces challange.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh's industrial growth faces challange.

text.p: Liquidity crisis in banks, restive labour unions and threats of political unrest have significantly contributed to Bangladesh's slow industrial growth, entrepreneurs and analysts said.
Although the banks made significant strides in recent months to recover bad loans, they do not expect any momentum in the industrial sector in the short run.

"There is acute problem of industrial financing at the moment. Develoment financing banks are now almost defunct. Their funds have dried up due to huge overdue loans," A.S.M. Quasem, President of Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told Reuters on Wednesday.

Opposition leader Begum Khaleda Zia said earlier this week her Bangladesh Nationalist Party was consulting smaller right-wing patries about launching a campaign for mid-term election to topple Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. The election is not due until 2001.
"Investors, especially in the private sector, are now watching (the political situation)," Quasem said.
Quasem said he did not see any prospect of industrial development in the short term.

"Unless the government restructures the DFIs (Development Financial Institutions) through strengthening of management and injecting fresh funds the industrial growth will suffer," he said in an interview.
The leading industrial bank, Bangladesh Shilpa Bank, has a huge number of approved projects lined up but no money.
"The bank is in very bad shape," said one senior Shilpa Bank official who declined to be identified.

The bank gave two billion taka ($45.3 million) credit in fiscal 1994/95 (July-June) against 12 billion taka worth of projects approved. The bank has since not been able to take up any fresh project. In 1995/96 it offered only one billion taka, bank officials said.
Quasem said: "Most of the projects were approved under political pressure."

Other entrepreneurs said the country's capital market could be a prospective source for industrial financing. But the capital market is still reeling from impacts of large scale price manipulations last year.
The government is now asking banks to form a consortium to finance industrial projects.
Finance Minister A.S.M.S. Kibria said last week the industrial sector could no longer get long-term loans from the commercial banks.

The banking crisis has haunted entrepreneurs since early this year when Bangladesh Bank (central bank) governor Lutfar Rahman Sarkar triggered an alarm by saying that the banking sector faced a severe liquidity churnch.
It prompted warnings of legal action against the loan defaulters. And this has brought some results.
The commercial banks have now 15 billion taka in excess liquidity rising from less than five billion in April.
Kibria said some of the loss-making industries could be liquidated.
"We will try to rehabilitate those sick industries which have potential, but if the efforts fail they will be liquidated," Kibria told a meeting of businessmen.
So far more than 5,000 industries have been closed down due to lack of working capital and mismanagement, said an industrialist.
"Industries can never be sick. It is the failure of the mangement, or faults in planning," Kibria said.

The entrepreneurs say the condition of public companies are even worse than the one managed by the private sector. Huge amounts of public money are being drained out to keep the loss-making industries running.
Bangladesh spends nearly $500 million annually in offering subsidies to state-owned enterprises, according to official figures.
Quasem said: "The government should either privatise the companies or liquidate them to stop bleeding of national resources."

But officials said the task is easier said than done, because powerful labour unions want the jobs protected after transfer of ownership of industries or handsome pay-off money for workers losing jobs.
Growth of Bangladesh's manufacturing sector dropped to 3.3 percent in fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) from 5.3 percent in 1995/96 and 8.6 percent in 1994/95.
